# Transitioning from Perpetual to Subscription: An Integrated Plan

---

## 1. Frame the Problem Correctly

Three facts change the shape of the answer:

**a) You are not building a recurring business from zero.** Maintenance revenue is already recurring — typically 40–50% of total revenue at a mature perpetual vendor. The transition affects only the *new license* line and the *pricing* of the existing maintenance stream. The trough is narrower than the headline suggests, and this is the single most important reframing for the board and the market.

**b) Migrating an existing maintenance customer is revenue-*accretive*, not dilutive.** A customer paying 20% maintenance on a $100 license pays $20/year. The same customer on subscription at $32–40/year is a 60–100% revenue uplift. Installed-base migration is the *filler* of the trough, not the cause of it. Only *new* business conversion creates dilution.

**c) The competitor didn't lose 20% because it switched. It lost 20% because it switched *to* customers rather than *with* them** — almost certainly some combination of forced conversion, maintenance end-of-life, a price uplift with no value uplift, and quota-carrying reps sent to strong-arm renewals. That failure mode is entirely avoidable and should be named explicitly in your design principles.

**Design principles (publish these internally and to customers):**
1. Perpetual means perpetual. No license is ever revoked, no maintenance stream is ever forcibly terminated.
2. Migration is always opt-in, always economically better for the customer than staying, and time-limited so that "better" decays.
3. Innovation is the pull, not price the push.
4. New business converts fast; installed base converts slowly.
5. Cash flow, not GAAP revenue, is the health metric during transition.
6. Nobody in the field should lose money for doing the right thing.
7. The trough is announced *before* it happens, quantified, and bounded.

---

## 2. Offer Architecture

**Three products in the price book, deliberately differentiated:**

| Offer | Who it's for | What's included | Rev rec |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Legacy Perpetual + Maintenance** | Existing customers who choose to stay | Current functionality, bug fixes, security patches, support, version upgrades within the existing product line. Price escalates at CPI + 2–3%, no more. | Unchanged |
| **Term Subscription (on-prem/private)** | Regulated, air-gapped, or infrastructure-bound customers | Full current product + all new modules + support. 1–3 year terms. | License component point-in-time under ASC 606 |
| **Cloud Subscription** | Default for all new business and migrators | Product + new AI/analytics/integration modules + managed operations + higher support tier + usage entitlements | Ratable |

**The critical product decision:** all *net-new* capability — new modules, cloud services, AI features, ecosystem integrations, new data connectors — ships to subscription only. Perpetual customers keep everything they bought, forever, fully supported. They simply stop receiving the *new* things. This is legally clean, ethically defensible, and creates the pull that makes migration voluntary.

**Do not** remove features, degrade support SLAs, or announce a maintenance sunset date. That is precisely the lever your competitor pulled.

**Use the term-license bridge deliberately.** Under ASC 606, the license component of an on-prem term license is recognized upfront on delivery. A three-year term deal recognizes a meaningful slug of revenue at signature. This materially shallows the reported trough while still building contracted recurring revenue. Two conditions: disclose upfront-recognized term license revenue as a separate line so you are never accused of engineering the optics, and treat it as a bridge, not a destination — the ARR and RPO disclosures are what the market will eventually price on.

---

## 3. The Installed-Base Migration Program ("Bridge")

Three paths, presented as customer choice:

**Path A — Stay.** No action. Perpetual license honored indefinitely. Maintenance continues at CPI+2–3%. Explicitly documented in writing to every account. This offer's *existence* is what prevents the 20% churn event.

**Path B — Convert (the recommended path).** Two economic instruments:

- **License Residual Credit.** Recognize the sunk investment. Grant a credit equal to a declining percentage of the original license fee — e.g., 40% if purchased in the last 2 years, 25% for 3–5 years, 10% for older — applied against the first 24 months of subscription. This is the single most effective answer to "we already bought this." It costs little (old licenses have near-zero residual economic value to you) and buys enormous goodwill.
- **Maintenance Credit.** 100% of prepaid maintenance credited pro rata.

- **Ramped pricing.** Year 1 at ~1.1× current maintenance spend, Year 2 at ~1.3×, Year 3 onward at ~1.5–1.6×. The customer's first-year cash outlay is nearly flat while receiving materially more product. You capture the uplift by year 3.
- **Five-year price protection**, capped uplift at renewal.
- **Free migration services** (fully subsidized in Wave 1, 50% in Wave 2, 0% thereafter).
- **Dual-run rights** for 12 months — keep running the perpetual install in parallel. Removes the technical risk objection almost entirely.
- **Perpetual fallback right:** if they cancel within 18 months, their perpetual license and maintenance are reinstated at the original terms. This is the fear-killer. Very few will use it; nearly all will notice it.

**Path C — Hybrid.** Keep perpetual for the core deployment, buy subscription for new sites/subsidiaries/modules. Common landing spot for large accounts; it converts them over 3–5 years through organic growth rather than through a decision.

**Urgency without coercion.** The Residual Credit and free migration services are available in **Wave 1 (first 12 months)** at full value, **Wave 2** at half, and **Wave 3** not at all. Scarcity of *incentive*, never scarcity of *support*, drives the timing.

**Sequencing of accounts.** Wave 1: high-NPS, cloud-ready, growth accounts and small/mid customers with low switching cost. Wave 2: mid-market breadth. Wave 3: strategic enterprise accounts with negotiated agreements — these go last, executive-sponsored, individually structured. Never open the migration conversation with your most entitled, most reference-able accounts in month one.

---

## 4. Pricing and the Shape of the Trough

**Anchor the conversion ratio.** Set new-business subscription price at roughly **35–42% of the old perpetual license fee per year**, which is ~2.0× the old maintenance rate. Customer breakeven vs. perpetual+maintenance lands at ~3 years, defensible against total cost of ownership including infrastructure and upgrade labor. Below ~30% you never recover the revenue; above ~50% you lose the value argument and adoption stalls.

**Illustrative model** (company at $500M: $200M license, $210M maintenance, $90M services; baseline growth 5%):

| | Baseline | Y1 | Y2 (trough) | Y3 | Y4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| % new business on subscription | — | 25% | 65% | 90% | 100% |
| % maintenance base migrated | — | 10% | 35% | 60% | 80% |
| Perpetual license rev | 200 | 150 | 70 | 20 | 0 |
| Maintenance rev | 210 | 193 | 137 | 84 | 42 |
| Subscription rev (new + migrated) | 0 | 24 | 131 | 278 | 430 |
| Services | 90 | 92 | 95 | 100 | 105 |
| **Total revenue** | **500** | **459** | **433** | **482** | **577** |
| vs. baseline trajectory | 500 / 525 / 551 / 579 / 608 | –13% | –21% | –17% | –5% |
| **Exiting ARR** | ~210 | ~275 | ~390 | ~520 | ~660 |

The story this table tells — and the story you tell the board — is: **reported revenue troughs ~13% below current in Year 2 and reclaims the prior peak in Year 4, while ARR grows monotonically every single quarter from day one.** Cumulative "deferred" revenue of roughly $300M is not lost; it is moved into future years at a higher lifetime value per customer.

**Levers to control trough depth** (rank-ordered by cost to the business):
1. Pace of new-business conversion by segment/geography — the primary throttle, adjustable quarterly.
2. Term-license mix with upfront recognition (shallower trough, no economic cost).
3. Migration wave sizing — faster migration = *more* revenue, so accelerate here if the trough is running deep.
